text: In the spring of 1944, southern England had become one vast military camp.
Hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers waited in tents, ports and airfields for the order to cross the English Channel.
Across the water, German forces held the coast of occupied France behind bunkers, mines and beach obstacles.
The invasion was set for the fifth of June, but a storm swept in over the Channel.
At Southwick House near Portsmouth, General Dwight Eisenhower listened to his weather forecasters.
They predicted a short break in the weather. Eisenhower gave the order. The invasion would begin on the sixth of June.
That night, thousands of paratroopers flew over Normandy in transport planes.
Many landed far from their targets, scattered across the fields and hedgerows in the dark.
In the town of Sainte-Mère-Église, American paratroopers fought through the streets. By dawn, the town was in their hands.
At sunrise, nearly seven thousand ships and landing craft appeared off the coast of Normandy.
The landings stretched across five beaches, code-named Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword.

text: At Omaha Beach, the landing craft dropped their ramps under heavy fire.
Soldiers waded through the surf and took cover behind steel obstacles as they pushed toward the bluffs.
By nightfall, about one hundred and fifty-six thousand Allied troops were ashore, at a cost of roughly ten thousand casualties.
In the weeks that followed, tanks and trucks rolled inland through the Norman countryside.
On the twenty-fifth of August, Paris was liberated.
The road to the end of the war in Europe had opened on the beaches of Normandy.
